name: The Ohatsuki Ginkgo of Yagisawa
species: Ohatsuki Ginkgo, a leaf-seed variant (Ginkgo biloba var. epiphylla)

location.address: Kamiyagisawa, Minobu, Minami-Koma-gun, Yamanashi, Japan (grounds of Yamajinja, also called Miyanomae Shrine)
location.neighbourhood: Kamiyagisawa, Minobu-cho, about 17 km south of Fujikawaguchiko's centre and about 1.7 km from fjk_002 (the Ohatsuki Ginkgo of Jotakuji Temple), in the same Shimoyama-area cluster of nationally designated Ohatsuki ginkgos

access: Free, on the grounds of Yamajinja (Miyanomae) Shrine in Kamiyagisawa, which welcomes visitors.
transport: About 15 minutes' walk from Hatakajima Station on the JR Minobu Line, or 5 minutes by car from Shimobe Onsen-Hayakawa IC.
story:
In the autumn of 2011 a male tree produced roughly forty seeds. They hung eight to ten metres up, on one branch of a ginkgo that had never fruited in its recorded history, because that single limb had quietly reversed sex on its own. Researchers took grafting and seedling permits at the University of Tokyo's botanical garden between 2015 and 2017 to work out what had happened, and that remains the freshest confirmation on record that the tree is alive and being watched.

It was already odd before that. Ohatsuki ginkgos carry their seeds on the leaf blade itself instead of on a stalk, a mutation rare enough that Japan has given the status of National Natural Monument to only seven of them. This one, on the grounds of Yamajinja shrine in Kamiyagisawa, is the only male of the seven, protected since July 1940. Botanists first described it in 1891, though the town's own page has also put that at 1896.

Nobody has ever dated it properly. Local tradition called it about 180 years old at the time of the 2011 fruiting, which puts it near two centuries now, and that is tradition rather than measurement. The trunk measures 3 metres round at chest height, 3.94 at the base, under 25 metres of crown. Another of the seven stands less than two kilometres away, at Jotakuji temple.

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter gold and drops in a day or two

name: Tarumi-no-Ozakura
species: Edo Higan Cherry (Prunus itosakura, syn. Prunus subhirtella var. ascendens)

location.address: Oya-cho Tarumi, Yabu City, Hyogo, Japan (a forest trail off the prefectural road along the Oya River, from Oya Junior High School)
location.neighbourhood: Oya-cho, Yabu City, roughly 20 km (mountain road, no public transport route found) from Asago, which we already publish; treated as its own single-tree place rather than joined to Asago

access: Free, on city-managed land. Reached by a roughly 15-minute walk on a forest trail from a small parking area (about 20 spaces); one-way traffic control and a temporary restroom are put in place for the blossom peak in early-to-mid April, when the site draws around 10,000 visitors. No public transport route found; a car is effectively required.
transport: No train or bus stop found serving the site; nearest access is by car via the prefectural road along the Oya River from Oya Junior High School, then a 15-minute walk.
story:
By 1993 this cherry was barely flowering. Now around 10,000 people come each April to watch it bloom.

The decline set in from 1967 and ran for three decades, until treatment began in 1997: the soil around the roots was improved and the tree was encouraged to throw out adventitious roots. By the city's 2020 survey it had recovered substantially. That survey measured it at 13.8 metres tall, 6.3 metres round at chest height and 7 metres at the root, which puts it among the ten oldest and thickest cherry trees recorded in Japan.

It is an Edo Higan, the long-lived species behind most of the country's ancient cherries, and a National Natural Monument since June 1951. Before the designation it was a lord's privilege: the feudal rulers of the Izushi Domain came here for their cherry-viewing, and in 1823 the domain's Confucian scholar Sakurai Sekimon named it Sensakura, the hermit's cherry. It now stands on the Silver Wagon Road, a Japan Heritage trail across Harima.

Its age is tradition rather than record. The sources say only that it is said to exceed a thousand years, and nobody has counted the rings.

Getting there takes a car and then a quarter of an hour on a forest trail. In blossom week the approach road runs one way and someone sets up a temporary toilet, which tells you how many people the walk is worth to.

best_time.label: early to mid April, when the blossom pulls thousands of people up the forest trail

name: Shogen-in no Sakasa Gashiwa

location.address: 273 Asahida, Hizume, Shiwa Town, Shiwa District, Iwate 028-3305, Japan (grounds of Shogen-in temple)
location.neighbourhood: Hizume, Shiwa Town, roughly 16 km (about 20-25 minutes by IGR Iwate Ginga Railway plus a 20-minute walk from Shiwa-Chuo Station, so 40-45 minutes door to door) from Morioka, which we already publish; too far to read as the same trip, so treated as its own single-tree place

access: Free, within the grounds (precincts) of Shogen-in, a working Soto Zen temple with its own visitor parking (room for about a dozen cars). Visitors are asked not to step directly under the canopy, to protect the soil the roots depend on.
transport: About 20 minutes' walk from Shiwa-Chuo Station on the IGR Iwate Ginga Railway (formerly JR Tohoku Line), which is roughly 20-25 minutes by train from Morioka.
story:
This oak looks as though someone planted it upside down. The trunk divides into four thick limbs at ground level, and rather than climbing they run outward along the earth before turning upward, so the branches read as roots that changed their minds. The name says it plainly: sakasa gashiwa, the inverted oak. The canopy off those limbs spreads 22 to 28 metres across.

It is the only Daimyo Oak in Japan under national protection, and the first oak of any species to be given that status, designated in December 1929 after the botanist Manabu Miyoshi of Tokyo Imperial University surveyed it in 1922.

The sourced estimates put it at roughly 300 years. The temple tells a longer story: its legend credits the planting to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and his son Yoshiie after the Former Nine Years' War in the eleventh century, and claims 700 years for the tree. That is legend, recorded as legend, and nobody has dated the oak by any other method.

The measurements depend on who took them and when. The town gives 630 cm around the base, 240 cm of trunk and 15 metres of height; a 1983 survey instead recorded 450 cm at the root, four limbs of about 2 metres each, and 12.2 metres tall. Different conventions, decades apart.

A tree enthusiast photographed it in bud in April 2025 and again in 2026. Shogen-in asks visitors not to step under the canopy, because that soil is what the roots live on.

name: The Yamamomo of Renchakuji
species: Japanese Bayberry (Myrica rubra, syn. Morella rubra)

location.address: 835 Tomido, Ito City, Shizuoka 413-0231, Japan (grounds of Renchakuji temple, on a terrace above the Jogasaki coast)
location.neighbourhood: Tomido, Ito City, on the Izu Peninsula, roughly 25 km from Atami, which we already publish; too far and too different a trip (Izu Kyuko Line plus a bus) to read as the same day, so treated as its own single-tree place

access: Free. The temple grounds are described by a tourism guide as 境内自由, freely open at all times. Reached by bus from Izu-Kogen Station (about 9 minutes to the Renchakuji stop) or by car; free parking for about 25 vehicles.
transport: Izu Kyuko Line to Izu-Kogen Station, then an eastbound bus toward the marine park, about 9 minutes to the Renchakuji stop, short walk from there.
story:
Japan's largest recorded yamamomo makes a good part of its own fertiliser. Bayberries host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in nodules on their roots, which is how the species holds on in thin coastal soil, and this one has reached 7.2 metres round on a terrace above the Jogasaki cliffs.

It is a female, 15 metres tall, the trunk splitting into three heavy limbs that carry a crown roughly 22 metres east to west and 18 north to south. Those are the figures taken when Japan made it a National Natural Monument in January 1999, and nobody appears to have measured it since. A tourism listing still described it in the present tense this year, which is reassuring rather than conclusive.

Its age is the part nobody agrees on. The cautious sources say over 300 years. A local story says over a thousand and has the tree brought here from the grove around the mausoleum of Emperor Heizei. Nothing in the evidence settles it, so the honest answer is somewhere in that wide band, and if you know better, tell us.

One thing it is not, whatever the archives suggest. This stretch of the Izu coast once held a designated bayberry colony at Tajima Village, and old maps of it circulate next to photographs of this tree. That colony was a separate designation and no longer exists. Renchakuji's bayberry is a single stock, standing on its own in temple grounds that are open at any hour.
